case_study_insert.main_stem: Harborne Vision Institute (HVI) is a private limited company in the private healthcare sector, specialising in ophthalmology, employing a workforce of 38. Founded in 2011 by Dr Lena Harborne, HVI operates two eye clinics in the Harborne district and uses a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. HVI plans to invest $920,000 in a second laser eye-surgery suite with energy-efficient solar panels, financed by a $600,000 ten-year bank loan and $320,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $306,000 a year, a variable cost of $14.50 a unit and a selling price of $40.00, and currently produces 78,000 units a year (treatment episodes). HVI faces two problems: nursing-staff turnover of 16% and rising patient complaints about waiting times.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Patient Report — Q3 2025: The two clinics delivered 19,500 treatment units last quarter at a rework rate of 1.3%, down from 2.6% a year ago. Patient complaints fell from 27 to 15 per month. A survey of 700 patients found that 59% would attend extended Saturday clinics and 44% would pay up to $25 more for same-day consultations. Average waiting time is 14 days. A training needs analysis shows 13 of 38 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new laser equipment; off-the-job training courses at the hospital college cost $820 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Harborne Vision Institute for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 3.75% to 4.5%, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.9% from $12.80 to $13.56 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills across private healthcare. (3) Ophthalmic lens and consumable costs have risen 8.8% year-on-year, healthcare inflation is running at 6.9%, and consumer spending on private eye care grew 4.6% in the same period.

questions.question_text: HVI plans to finance part of its laser expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for HVI of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using retained profit costs HVI nothing in interest or repayments, protecting cash flow at a time when it already carries fixed costs of $306,000 a year and a $600,000 bank loan commitment. Every dollar not paid to a lender can absorb the 8.8% rise in ophthalmic lens and consumable costs, helping HVI hold its $40.00 selling price and protect the $25.50 contribution per treatment unit without squeezing patients or margins.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral and repayment risk attached to a bank loan, so the $320,000 is available without putting the new $920,000 laser eye-surgery suite at risk of repossession if demand disappoints. It also preserves Dr Lena Harborne's ownership and control, since no external lender can impose conditions on how the second suite is staffed or run. Retained profit is also flexible — it carries no fixed monthly repayment schedule, unlike the loan, which matters while the 16% nursing-staff turnover is being addressed and waiting times stabilise.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Harborne Vision Institute and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: HVI is launching laser eye surgery at its second suite. Consider a national television campaign, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should HVI choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Television campaign: A national television campaign would put HVI's laser service in front of millions of viewers very quickly and build instant brand awareness across the country. However, HVI is a 38-employee ophthalmology clinic funding a $920,000 expansion; national production and airtime costs are extremely high, and most of the audience would live outside HVI's referral catchment or not be suitable laser candidates, so a large share of spend would be wasted. Television is also untargeted — many viewers neither need nor want elective eye surgery.

Local radio sponsorship: Local radio is far cheaper, reaches HVI's immediate community repeatedly, and suits time-sensitive, appointment-led messages such as same-day consultations and extended Saturday clinics. Its limitation is narrow reach; patients already travel from beyond the Harborne district for laser surgery, so a local station alone cannot fill a second surgery suite or build awareness of a county-wide referral base.

Social media influencer marketing: Working with trusted local health and lifestyle influencers targets exactly the 59% of surveyed patients who would attend extended Saturday clinics and the 44% who would pay up to $25 more for same-day consultations. Cost per reached patient is low, engagement is measurable, and the eco-conscious, health-focused positioning of the new suite with solar panels can be shown directly. Results build more slowly than TV and depend on influencer credibility, so content must be medically accurate.

Recommendation: HVI should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the precise segment already identified in its research (59% and 44%), costs far less than television for a 38-person business, scales better than local radio, and reinforces the clinic's modern, patient-centred image. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a two-site clinic; local radio is rejected as the lead channel because its reach is too narrow for county-wide laser referrals, though short local bursts could support the launch. Influencers alone lack mass reach, so HVI should pair them with its own patient-referral programme and in-clinic leaflets.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of HVI with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of HVI with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: HVI's nursing-staff turnover has reached 16% and patient complaints about waiting times are rising. Explain two benefits for HVI of its democratic leadership style.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives HVI's 38 staff a genuine voice in how rotas, triage protocols and the new laser suite are organised, satisfying social and esteem needs (Maslow) and increasing job satisfaction. Nurses who help shape patient-flow and waiting-list processes are more likely to attend consistently and stay in post, directly attacking HVI's 16% nursing-staff turnover rate and helping stabilise the 14-day average waiting time that is driving complaints.

Point 2: Involving staff in decisions generates practical suggestions from the people who handle patients daily, improving quality and pushing the 1.3% rework rate down further while complaints fall (27 to 15 per month). Higher involvement raises commitment and lowers turnover, saving the $820 per employee retraining cost at the hospital college and protecting output of 78,000 treatment units a year, keeping the fall in rework from 2.6% to 1.3% on track while the second surgery suite beds in and the 13 under-trained staff complete their laser training.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to HVI's turnover, waiting times, rework rate and output.

questions.question_text: HVI must train 13 clinic staff to operate the new laser equipment. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the hospital college. Which should HVI choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training alongside experienced surgeons and nurses in HVI's own theatres is directly relevant to its laser machines, protocols and patient-safety checklists, costs nothing in course fees, and keeps the 13 staff productive while they learn. This protects the last quarter's delivery of 19,500 treatment units and the effort behind the fall in rework from 2.6% to 1.3%. Drawbacks are that trainers are clinical staff whose own patient work suffers, bad habits can pass between colleagues, and formal certification is limited — an issue if commissioners or insurers demand written evidence of competence on the laser suite before it opens.

Off-the-job training: The hospital college course at $820 per employee gives structured, up-to-date laser-safety content and a recognised certificate for all 13 staff, costing $10,660 in total — affordable against a $920,000 expansion. It removes clinical staff from the clinics, however, reducing short-term capacity and potentially lengthening the 14-day waiting time, and the generic college content may not match HVI's exact laser settings, so follow-up on-site coaching would still be required.

Decision: HVI should choose on-the-job training for the initial rollout, supported by off-the-job college places for two senior nurses who can then cascade laser-safety practice to the rest. On-the-job training is cheapest, machine-specific and avoids further capacity loss while turnover is already 16% and the waiting list is a complaint driver. Full off-the-job training is rejected because withdrawing 13 staff and spending $10,660 up front would deepen the 14-day waiting-time problem; HVI can add college certification later once the suite stabilises and the turnover rate comes down.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to HVI.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of HVI.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of HVI with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption, certification and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how HVI's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $306,000 ÷ ($40.00 − $14.50) = $306,000 ÷ $25.50 = 12,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 12,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $40.00 − $14.50 = $25.50. Answer: contribution per unit is $25.50.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways HVI's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. HVI's managers can compare the 12,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 78,000 units to confirm the clinics are comfortably profitable, with a margin of safety of 66,000 units, informing whether the new laser suite can be staffed and opened ahead of schedule.
2. Contribution per unit of $25.50 lets managers model the effect of an extended Saturday clinic premium, for example raising the average price by $2 to $42.00 would lift contribution to $27.50, letting managers judge whether extra hours would still clear the $306,000 fixed costs and cover the $600,000 loan repayments.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $306,000 and contribution per unit helps managers set treatment-volume targets used to justify the second suite's debt service and to test whether the 59% of patients willing to attend Saturday clinics can be converted into enough sessions to keep the suite profitable.
4. Managers can use unit cost data ($306,000 ÷ 78,000 units + $14.50 = $18.42 a unit) to benchmark performance across quarters, identify waste driving the rising waiting-time complaints, and decide whether to renegotiate lens and consumable supply contracts amid the 8.8% input-cost inflation.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 12,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $25.50 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 66,000 units vs 78,000-unit output; pricing and Saturday-clinic premium modelling vs $306,000 fixed costs; loan-repayment feasibility for the $920,000 laser expansion; and unit-cost benchmarking at $18.42 to tackle waste and input inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate HVI's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, the profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has HVI's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 35.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 20.0%
ROCE 2024 = 10.0%
ROCE 2025 = 15.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit $910,000 on revenue $2,600,000 (cost of sales $1,690,000); 2025 gross profit $1,404,000 on revenue $3,120,000 (cost of sales $1,716,000). 2024 operating profit $312,000; 2025 operating profit $624,000. 2024 capital employed $3,120,000; 2025 capital employed $4,160,000. Interest payable rose from $26,000 to $38,000, reflecting the ten-year bank loan funding the laser suite.

Evaluation: Performance improved strongly. Gross profit grew $494,000 (54.3%) as revenue rose $520,000 and the cost of sales share of revenue fell from 65.0% to 55.0%, helped by the rework rate falling from 2.6% to 1.3% and complaints from 27 to 15 a month. Operating profit grew 100.0% ($312,000 to $624,000), well ahead of revenue growth of 20.0%, so overheads were absorbed more efficiently across two clinics. Capital employed rose $1,040,000 on the laser suite with solar panels, yet the return on that capital still strengthened because the suite feeds high-margin elective procedures. However, interest charges are rising with the loan and the base-rate move from 3.75% to 4.5%, and the 8.8% lens-and-consumable inflation could reverse part of the cost-of-sales improvement if suppliers pass increases on faster than HVI can adjust prices.

Conclusion: Yes, HVI's financial performance has improved. Revenue, gross profit and operating profit all grew more than comfortably, cost control genuinely improved rather than riding on price rises alone, and the return on capital employed climbed from 10.0% to 15.0% with the expansion executed cleanly. The judgement is not risk-free — borrowing is costlier after the base-rate rise and input inflation is running well above price rises — so HVI should monitor the laser suite's ramp-up closely, protect consumable margins and keep tightening waiting-time and turnover metrics.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost of sales, overheads and capital employed movements and a justified conclusion on whether HVI's financial performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for HVI of installing energy-efficient solar panels at its clinics.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Solar panels cut HVI's electricity bills across two clinics, directly lowering the $306,000 fixed-cost base and freeing cash to fund the $920,000 laser suite rather than diverting it to energy suppliers. They also strengthen HVI's image with health-conscious patients — the same audience behind the 59% Saturday-clinic and 44% same-day-consultation demand — signalling that modern private care can be delivered responsibly, which supports retention of private patients and differentiation from NHS alternatives.

Disadvantage: The panels add an upfront cost on top of an already stretched $920,000 project funded partly by a $600,000 bank loan, increasing immediate cash strain and the amount HVI must borrow or repay. Installation can also disrupt clinical sessions and the 14-day waiting-time target: roof works above surgery theatres raise safety and continuity-of-care risks, and any fault or maintenance visit takes rooms offline, which HVI cannot afford while nursing-staff turnover is 16% and full laser capacity is not yet proven.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to HVI's costs, demand data and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.5%, the 5.9% minimum wage increase and the 8.8% rise in input costs will affect HVI. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (3.75% to 4.5%): If HVI's $600,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage point rise adds about $4,500 a year to financing costs — real but modest next to $306,000 of fixed costs. Higher rates also make further borrowing for clinic number three more expensive, could raise renewal quotes on the hire-purchase-style equipment leases, and may make patients more cautious about elective procedures, softening the 4.6% growth in private eye-care spending. HVI can partly shield itself by fixing the loan rate.

Minimum wage increase (5.9%, to $13.56 per hour): HVI employs 38 staff, mostly nurses, technicians and reception alongside clinical leadership; clinical pay sits well above minimum wage, but support, cleaning and administrative roles are affected. If even 15 of the 38 staff sit near the minimum wage on roughly 40-hour weeks, the 5.9% rise adds roughly $1,250 per affected worker per year — around $19,000 a year — on top of the 16% turnover already inflating recruitment and the $820-per-head retraining bill. The impact is material but concentrated on the support-staff budget.

Input cost inflation (8.8% ophthalmic lens and consumables): HVI's variable cost of $14.50 a unit is dominated by lenses, viscoelastics and sterile consumables. An 8.8% rise on the consumable share (say 60% of the variable cost, $8.70) adds roughly $0.77 per treatment unit; at 78,000 units a year that is about $60,000 a year, cutting contribution per unit from $25.50 toward $24.73 and eroding roughly 3% of margin. The private eye-care market grew 4.6%, so passing on only part of the increase risks a competitive backlash while absorbing it all bites directly into ROCE.

Conclusion: The 8.8% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact. It strikes every one of the 78,000 units sold, totalling roughly $60,000 a year and steadily eroding the $25.50 contribution margin that justifies the $920,000 laser suite. The minimum wage rise is the second most serious risk, concentrated in support roles and amplified by 16% turnover, while the interest-rate increase is the smallest in cash terms (about $4,500 a year on the drawn loan) and can be managed by fixing the rate. Even so, HVI must address all three — negotiate consumable contracts, redesign support-role rosters productively, and review the loan structure — or the improved cost-of-sales performance shown in Appendix 2 will unwind.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to HVI.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on HVI's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of HVI with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
